newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Philippine peso move rattles regional currencies.
newsitem.headline: Philippine peso move rattles regional currencies.

text.p: Southeast Asian currencies were shaken on Friday by the Philippines' shock move to effectively devalue the peso after it had repeatedly denied this week it would take such a step.
The Philippine central bank made the surprise announcement in early Friday trading, saying it would allow the peso to trade in a wider range against the U.S. dollar, with immediate effect.
The bank gave no indication of what the wider range would be.
Dealers saw the move as the second de facto devaluation of an Asian currency in less than two weeks.

The Thai baht's managed float on July 2 was viewed as an effective devaluation with the currency losing some 15 percent of its value as a result. Thailand's move came after speculators attacked its currency.
The peso shed over 11 percent to 29.450 to the dollar in an immediate reaction to the news, before the Bankers Association of the Philippines halted peso-dollar trades for the day.
Dealers said the news, though widely seen as inevitable, did little to restore the already fragile confidence of investors and foreign fund managers in the region.
"They had very little choice anyway. It was just a matter of time, especially if all the stronger economies in this region are suffering. What else can they do," a Singapore dealer said.
In Thailand, the baht was hammered once again in just over a week after its own de facto devaluation, as the peso news spurred heavy demand for the U.S. dollar.
"It has definitely been hurt by the Philippine peso attacks. Speculators are focusing on both the Philippine and Thai currencies," a dealer at a Thai bank in Bangkok said.

The baht on Friday hit its weakest level to date of 29.900 to the dollar against 29.100/29.200 late on Thursday. It was quoted at 29.900/29.950 in the onshore market and 29.350/29.450 offshore at 0415 GMT.

But dealers said the baht's weakness was contained by Thai central bank measures, implemented when the currency came under speculative attack in mid-May, to block foreign speculators' access to local baht supplies.
Dealers said they had not seen any signs on Friday that the Thai central bank had stepped in to defend the baht.
In Indonesia, the rupiah steadied after being jolted early on the Philippine news but remained weak as players began to assess morning's developments.
"We see some dollar selling. I think offshore operators are taking profits as there is no problem with the rupiah," a European bank dealer in Jakarta said.
Spot rupiah was at around 2,435.5/36.5 at 0415 GMT against an early low of 2,437.0. It opened at 2,432.5/33.5.

The Malaysian ringgit also came under pressure but dealers said its downside was limited as the market was already holding long dollar positions. They said selling was also reined by signs of the central bank's presence.
Dealers said the ringgit weakened to 2.4980 against the dollar but Bank Negara Malaysia was calling banks to check rates during the currency's move to that level.
"They've been around the whole day but they don't need to (act). Nobody's doing anything," the Singapore dealer said.
He said the ringgit's losses would be limited to 2.5050 to the dollar.
The Singapore dollar however, remained relatively calm and firmed slightly, benefiting as usual on signs of regional instability. At 0530 GMT, the Singapore dollar was at 1.4340 to the U.S. dollar.
